# True or false: Data

Ownership, classification, quality and privacy. Most data problems are ownership problems; see which common habits make them worse.

10 statements (Foundation 5, Standard 5). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area data`.

### 1. Copying the production database to staging is the best way to get realistic test data.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Staging usually has weaker access controls, so personal data copied there is exposed. Use synthetic data or approved masking with a deletion date. Keep production personal data in production.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md](../../playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md)

</details>

### 2. Marking all data as confidential is the safest classification policy.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** When everything is confidential, the label tells nobody what really needs protection. Use the definitions for public, internal, confidential and restricted. Over-classifying hides what matters and slows every request.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-governance.md](../../playbook/data/data-governance.md)

</details>

### 3. Data mesh is the recommended default model for organising data work in most organisations.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The playbook treats data mesh, as described by Zhamak Dehghani, as an option for large organisations with many domains and strong platform support. Start with ownership by the team that produces the data. Fix ownership and contracts first; adopt mesh only if scale requires it.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-governance.md](../../playbook/data/data-governance.md)

</details>

### 4. Data quality problems should be fixed at the source rather than by each team that uses the data.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** When every consumer cleans data in its own way, two dashboards show two different numbers. Fixing it once at the source corrects it for everyone. Publish the rule in the data contract.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-quality.md](../../playbook/data/data-quality.md)

</details>

### 5. A data contract can be checked in CI so that a breaking schema change fails the producer's build.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A data contract is an agreement in version control between the producing team and the teams that use the data. Checking it in the producer's CI catches a breaking change before it reaches consumers. Version contracts with Semantic Versioning.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-quality.md](../../playbook/data/data-quality.md)

</details>

### 6. A data protection impact assessment can be written after launch, once the design is settled.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A DPIA (GDPR Article 35) exists to change the design while that is still cheap. Do it before high-risk processing starts, such as profiling or AI on personal data. Update it when the processing changes.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md](../../playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md)

</details>

### 7. Keeping full personal data in logs for years is fine as long as only engineers can read the logs.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Logs are copied widely and kept long, so they quietly become one of the largest stores of personal data. Mask personal data in the logging library. Keep raw logs for a short period.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md](../../playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md)

</details>

### 8. GDPR Article 25 expects data protection to be built into the design of a system, not added later.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Article 25 covers data protection by design and by default. Building privacy in from the start costs far less than retrofitting it after a breach or a complaint. Collect only what you need and delete it on schedule.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md](../../playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md)

</details>

### 9. Confidential or restricted data should go to an external AI service only with the data owner's approval and a contract covering use, retention and location.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Sending data to a hosted model is a transfer to a supplier. The data owner decides whether that use is allowed. The contract must say how the data is used, how long it is kept and where it is stored.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-governance.md](../../playbook/data/data-governance.md)

</details>

### 10. A retention period written in a policy document is enough to meet deletion obligations.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A policy that nothing enforces leaves the data in place. Run automated deletion jobs and monitor that they succeed. Make sure you can also find and delete all of one person's data on request.

Read more: [playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md](../../playbook/data/data-security-and-privacy.md)

</details>
